newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-OECD sees exports fuelling German growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OECD sees exports fuelling German growth.

text.p: High unemployment and weak domestic consumption will continue to plague the German economy this year but exports and business spending should fuel respectable growth, the OECD forecast on Thursday.

"Exports grew strongly in the second half of 1996 and forward indicators suggest that they will, together with business investment, remain the main source of growth," the Paris-based think-tank said in its twice-yearly report.

While overall prospects for the 29 OECD member countries were good, with three percent growth seen for 1997, the OECD said German growth would lag somewhat at 2.2 percent amid poor consumption and stubornly high joblessness.
"The weakness of employment growth in much of the European Union may revive questions of whether a 'jobless recovery' is in prospect in some countries, notably Germany," the OECD said.
Germany's unemployment rate -- now hovering around levels not seen since the 1930s recession -- is projected to rise further this year before easing slightly in 1998.

Joblessness will rise to 11.1 percent or 4.3 million people this year, from 10.3 percent or 4.0 million in 1996, the report said. The jobless total would then fall back to 4.2 million, or 10.9 percent, in 1998.
On the plus side, the report said continued low inflation and interest rate levels as well as improved productivity would help offset woes on the labour front.

"International competitiveness and profitability have improved with the weakening of the deutschemark vis a vis the U.S. dollar, a moderate wage round and a marked improvement in productivity growth," the OECD said.
"Overall, monetary conditions constitute a favourable basis for growth to pick up."

The report predicted that Germany's budget deficit -- along with that of France and Italy -- would be 3.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1997, heralding a clear overshooting of Maastricht Treaty goals in the test year for monetary union.
"Expectations about the ability of countries to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of the year could have unpredictable confidence and financial markets effects."
Other future risks included any weakening in foreign markets, which would have serious negative impact on export-dependent Germany.
Overall, the OECD said prospects for even faster German growth than current forecasts indicated largely depended on consumer confidence returning.
Agreements on a tax reform in 1998, currently a hot topic here, could have benefit in this regard.
Key OECD forecasts for Germany (Percentage changes, seasonally adjusted at annual rates)
GDP at market prices 1.4pct 2.2 pct 2.8 pct
GDP deflator 1.0 pct 1.2 pct 1.1 pct
Industrial production 0.1 pct 2.6 pct 3.2 pct
Unemployment rate 10.3 pct 11.1 pct 10.9 pct
